{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=failure+modes+of+instruction-following+in+AI+systems+when+human+objectives+are+contextually+inadequate&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7433399\", \"title\": [\"When Agentic AI Breaks Software Quality Assurance: Failure Modes, Reliability Risks, and Governance Strategies for Autonomous Testing Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing software quality assurance from a predominantly human-directed activity into an increasingly autonomous process in which AI systems can generate tests, execute programs, interpret failures, modify test suites, and iteratively refine their actions. While these capabilities promise substantial improvements in testing speed, coverage, and engineering productivity, they also introduce a distinct class of quality risks. An autonomous testing agent can produce a technically executable test that encodes an incorrect assumption, misinterpret a failure, optimize for coverage rather than meaningful defect detection, or repeatedly reinforce an erroneous testing strategy. This article examines these risks through an integrative review of research on large language models (LLMs), automated software testing, AI-assisted software engineering, and AI governance. The analysis identifies six interconnected failure modes: erroneous test generation, defective test oracles, autonomous error propagation, coverage-driven quality illusion, contextual and repository misunderstanding, and governance and accountability failure. The article argues that the central challenge is not simply whether AI can generate valid tests, but whether autonomous testing systems can maintain trustworthy quality judgments under uncertainty. Drawing on empirical evidence from recent studies of ChatGPT, LLM-based test generation, TestGen-LLM, and software-engineering agents, the article proposes a risk-based governance model built around bounded autonomy, independent verification, traceability, human checkpoints, continuous monitoring, and explicit escalation mechanisms. The findings suggest that enterprise adoption should treat agentic testing as a controlled socio-technical system rather than a replacement for software …

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=How+do+path-dependent+preference+formation+and+attractor+states+manifest+in+recurrent+human-AI+feedback+loops%3F&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.31219/osf.io/c4e7r\", \"title\": [\"How human-AI feedback loops alter human perceptual, emotional and social judgements\"], \"abstract\": \"

Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are rapidly advancing, enhancing human capabilities across various domains spanning from finance to medicine. Despite their numerous advantages, AI systems can exhibit biases in judgments ranging from perception to emotion. Here, in a series of experiments (N=1,201), we reveal a feedback loop where human-AI interactions alter processes underlying human perceptual, emotional and social judgements, subsequently amplifying biases in humans. This amplification is significantly greater than observed in interactions between humans, due both to the tendency of AI systems to amplify biases and to how humans perceive AI systems. Participants are often unaware of the extent of the AI’s influence, rendering them more susceptible to it. These findings reveal a mechanism wherein AI systems amplify human biases, which are further internalized by humans during human-AI interactions, triggering a snowball effect where small errors in judgment escalate into much larger ones.
